greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. May the grace and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who calls us to be the light of the world, be with you all.
penitential:
Lord Jesus, you are the light that shines in the darkness. Lord, have mercy.
Christ Jesus, you call us to carry our cross and follow you. Christ, have mercy.
Lord Jesus, you promise that we shall see the bounty of the Lord in the land of the living. Lord, have mercy.
psalm_response: The Lord is my light and my salvation.
homily:
We begin today not with a complex doctrine, but with the image of a foundation. Think of a builder standing on a plot of land, looking at the dirt, the stones, and the blueprints spread out before him. He is thinking about gravity, about the seasons, about how to build something that will not collapse when the wind rises. He is calculating the cost of the stone, the depth of the trench, and the strength of the mortar. It is a moment of quiet, intense focus. It is a moment of total honesty. Before the first brick is laid, he must know if he has what it takes to finish the work. Jesus speaks of this in the Gospel today—the builder, the king, the one who must count the cost of discipleship. It is an image of radical, sober commitment.

I want you to hold onto this image: the foundation. It is the place where we decide what we will build our lives upon, and it is the place where we discover what is truly strong enough to hold us when the world shifts beneath our feet.

Let us speak the truth of the heart before we look for the comfort. Alan, Thao, Ryan, and all of you who carry the light of Benjamin Vo in your souls: it has been four months since Ben crossed the threshold of this world. We know the reality of your quiet house. We know the moments when the silence becomes a weight, when the habits of a lifetime—the coding, the aviation spotting, the simple joy of a shared meal—are suddenly interrupted by the sharp, cold realization that he is not there in the way he once was. You are grieving. You are carrying a cross that feels far too heavy for human shoulders. You are allowed to be tired. You are allowed to be angry at the unfairness of a world that takes a boy of such brilliant promise. You are allowed to be human.

There is a temptation, when we carry this kind of sorrow, to look back at the path we walked and wonder if we missed a sign. We wonder if we could have seen something earlier, or done something differently, or if we failed in some hidden way. Let us lift that stone from your hearts right now. You missed nothing. You were the parents and the brother that Benjamin was given. You loved him with a completeness that filled his fifteen years with the richness of the world. You walked the globe with him, you shared the meals, you witnessed the brilliance of his mind and the gentleness of his spirit. God does not accuse you, and you must not accuse yourselves. Some sorrows in this fragile world arrive entirely beyond human reach, untouched by anything anyone did or failed to do. You are not to blame. Let that heavy stone fall to the ground; you are absolved. You were faithful. You were present. You were love in action.

Now, let the Gospel break in. Jesus is not asking us to count the cost so that we might walk away in fear. He is asking us to count the cost so that we might realize that we cannot build this tower on our own. He is inviting us to build our lives on the foundation of His grace. When he says, ‘Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple,’ he is not inviting us to a life of misery. He is inviting us to a life of profound, shared reality. He is saying, ‘I have already carried the cross. I have already counted the cost. I have already laid the foundation in my own blood. Now, come and build your life on me.’

Benjamin was a boy who understood the beauty of a well-laid plan. Think of his brilliant, searching mind—the way he mastered mathematics, the way he dived into the complexities of cloud infrastructure, or how he coded his own games in his GitHub repository. He loved the logic of things. He loved the way a system could be built to function perfectly. But think of the gentleness of his spirit, which was the true architecture of his life. Think of that moment when he offered his entire piggy bank to help his uncle William, who was suffering from strokes. He didn't need to break it open, he didn't need to empty it; the offer itself was the revelation of his character. It was the movement of a soul that already understood that we are here to give, not to hoard. That is the boy you raised. That is the boy who is now at the banquet of heaven, interceding for you. He is not a memory; he is a living soul, fully alive in the love of God. He is a guest who has already taken his seat, and he is waiting for the rest of his family to arrive.

Ryan, you are a brother who carries a unique, holy weight. You know the memories better than anyone. You know the games you coded, the dreams you shared, the simple, everyday life of being brothers. You are not just a brother who remains; you are a brother who continues the story. When you look at the sky, when you think of the future, remember that you are not doing it alone. You are carrying the legacy of his joy. You are a witness to the world that love is not a finite resource. It is a well that never runs dry. Keep being the boy who reaches out. Keep being the one who values the small, human moments. You are a vital part of this family of four, and your life is a testament to the fact that love is the most durable thing we possess.

We hear in the letter to the Philippians today: ‘Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For God is the one who, for his good purpose, works in you both to desire and to work.’ This is the mystery of our faith. We are not the ones building the tower alone. God is the architect. God is the one who provides the resources. He is the one who works in us to desire and to act. Even in your grief, even in the moments when you feel you have nothing left to give, God is working in you. He is the one who gives you the strength to wake up, the strength to speak his name, the strength to hope. He is the one who is holding you when you feel like you are falling.

There is a peace that comes from knowing that we are held. It is not a peace that takes away the pain, but it is a peace that keeps us from being destroyed by it. It is the peace of knowing that Benjamin is waiting. He is waiting in the light, he is waiting in the place where there is no more struggling, no more darkness, only the clear, bright presence of the Father. He is waiting for you with that same sweet, gentle smile that you remember so vividly. That smile is the sign that the work is going well. That smile is the promise that the reunion is certain. He is a light in the world, just as St. Paul says, shining in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, and he is shining for you.

So, what do you carry out the door today? Not a summary, not a heavy burden, but one small, doable thing: when the grief rises and the house feels too quiet, pause. Close your eyes. Imagine the Lord reaching into the silence, and imagine Benjamin smiling at you from the other side. Let yourself be gathered. Trust that you are held. And walk out into the world with the quiet, unshakeable hope that the love you share is the most powerful force in the universe. It is stronger than death. It is more enduring than time. And it is the very thing that will bring you home to each other. You are not a broken family. You are a family of four, and you are being held in the palm of God's hand. Keep your heart open to that truth. Keep your eyes on the light. And remember that he is watching over you, always, with love that knows no end. Amen.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that you are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love you above all things, and I desire to receive you into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive you sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace you as if you were already there and unite myself wholly to you. Never permit me to be separated from you. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may his face shine upon you and give you peace. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
standing_petitions: For our beloved Benjamin Vo, and for all who have gone before us, that they may rest forever in the radiant light of Christ's peace.
For all who are grieving, especially Ben's family and friends, that God may console their hearts and grant them the hope of a glorious reunion.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
My beloved, obedient as you have always been,
not only when I am present but all the more now when I am absent,
work out your salvation with fear and trembling.
For God is the one who, for his good purpose,
works in you both to desire and to work.
Do everything without grumbling or questioning,
that you may be blameless and innocent,
children of God without blemish
in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation,
among whom you shine like lights in the world,
as you hold on to the word of life,
so that my boast for the day of Christ may be
that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.
But, even if I am poured out as a libation
upon the sacrificial service of your faith,
I rejoice and share my joy with all of you.
In the same way you also should rejoice and share your joy with me.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (1a) The Lord is my light and my salvation.
The LORD is my light and my salvation;
whom should I fear?
The LORD is my life’s refuge;
of whom should I be afraid?
R. The Lord is my light and my salvation.
One thing I ask of the LORD;
this I seek:
To dwell in the house of the LORD
all the days of my life,
That I may gaze on the loveliness of the LORD
and contemplate his temple.
R. The Lord is my light and my salvation.
I believe that I shall see the bounty of the LORD
in the land of the living.
Wait for the LORD with courage;
be stouthearted, and wait for the LORD.
R. The Lord is my light and my salvation.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
Great crowds were traveling with Jesus,
and he turned and addressed them,
“If anyone comes to me without hating his father and mother, 
wife and children, brothers and sisters,
and even his own life,
he cannot be my disciple.
Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me
cannot be my disciple.
Which of you wishing to construct a tower
does not first sit down and calculate the cost
to see if there is enough for its completion? 
Otherwise, after laying the foundation
and finding himself unable to finish the work
the onlookers should laugh at him and say,
‘This one began to build but did not have the resources to finish.’ 
Or what king marching into battle would not first sit down
and decide whether with ten thousand troops
he can successfully oppose another king
advancing upon him with twenty thousand troops? 
But if not, while he is still far away,
he will send a delegation to ask for peace terms. 
In the same way,
everyone of you who does not renounce all his possessions
cannot be my disciple.”

Down here, Mom and I are crying more and more each day. A piece of my heart feels completely dead without you, Ben. Please watch over us, pray for your mom, your brother Ryan, and me, and give us the strength to keep going. We love you forever
